Dark Matter: The Universe’s Invisible Dominator

Anyone passionate about astrophysics or cosmology knows that, for several decades, scientists have been forced to hypothesize the existence of vast quantities of matter in galaxies—particles that remain unknown in Earth’s laboratories, but whose mass and gravitational pull outweigh everything else humanity has detected. These exotic particles neither emit nor absorb light, or do so only very weakly. Hence, the fitting name: dark matter. This mysterious component of the observable Universe seems essential to explain not only how stars and clouds of matter move within galaxies, but even how entire galaxies behave within clusters.

Dark matter also seems needed to describe certain features of the famous “fossil radiation”: the cosmic microwave background, or CMB—the lingering light from the end of the Big Bang in which all of observable space is still bathed. Honestly, it’s long been clear that it’s nearly impossible to explain the properties of the CMB (studied in detail by the European Space Agency’s Planck mission) without invoking dark matter, unless you’re ready to toss out the gravitational laws of Newton and Einstein.

To Modify Gravity, Or Not?

Despite this, some astrophysicists have suggested that instead of introducing an entirely new kind of matter, perhaps we should just tweak Newton’s celestial mechanics in particular situations. In other words, maybe the acceleration of a star or galaxy due to a gravitational field shouldn’t always decrease with the square of the distance (the famous 1/R2 law).

This line of thinking gave rise to the MOND theory (Modified Newtonian Dynamics), first proposed in the early 1980s by Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom. It’s a framework that brings together various approaches, all essentially trying to adjust Newtonian dynamics—something researchers like French astrophysicist Benoit Famaey have explored in depth.

Showdown: Dark Matter vs. Modified Gravity

For almost 40 years, astrophysicists have debated: should we introduce entirely new particles (the famous dark matter), or should we modify the laws of Newton to explain the behavior of galaxies, galaxy clusters, and even the oldest light in the Universe—the CMB? Dark matter has generally offered the best, most consistent explanation, yet the idea of modified gravity always lurks in the background, especially when considering galaxy rotations.

Recently, new findings seemed to back dark matter’s case, especially thanks to data from ESA’s Gaia satellite and NASA’s Fermi telescope. But is dark matter truly defeating every alternative, especially MOND?

In the debate, a Korean researcher published a paper apparently supporting MOND, challenging dark matter. Yet, using that same Gaia data on binary star systems, a different research team spectacularly refuted MOND.

The Atacama Test: Cracking the Modified Gravity Hypothesis

The story doesn’t end there! To get more specific, according to MOND, as long as distances aren’t too enormous, gravity (and the resulting acceleration) still drops off with 1/R2. But below a certain universal acceleration threshold, this no longer holds.

This very hypothesis was tested using years of data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), a six-meter radio telescope perched atop Cerro Toco in Chile’s Atacama Desert, 16,990 feet (5,190 meters) above sea level. Although ACT shut down in September 2022 after 15 years capturing photons from the Big Bang, analysis of its massive dataset on the CMB is still underway—and making waves.

More broadly, this data has allowed scientists to put Einstein’s general relativity to the test on the largest spatial scales ever attempted. How? By studying the movements of thousands of galaxy clusters, separated by tens of millions of light-years and interacting gravitationally. To do this, physicists use the famous Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect—not its thermal version, but the often-overlooked kinematic variant.

  • Galaxy clusters are immersed in extremely hot plasma teeming with fast-moving electrons.
  • As these electrons collide with CMB photons, they inject energy into some of them, distorting the blackbody spectrum of the background radiation.
  • This effect can be measured thermally, but the kinematic version depends on the clusters’ overall motion (like two stars orbiting each other).
  • By examining these effects separately, astrophysicists can test whether accelerations fit MOND’s expectations or follow classical gravity.

Patricio A. Gallardo from the University of Pennsylvania (USA) and colleagues played this high-stakes game, publishing their results in Physical Review Letters (with an open-access version on arXiv). Their conclusion? MOND is refuted with better than 3 sigma certainty—a discovery worthy of a headline.

However, there’s a twist. The researchers concede a subtlety known as the External Field Effect (EFE): the influence of external gravitational fields (like those from many nearby galaxy clusters or ordinary matter spread between them) on the internal accelerations of a physical system. This could potentially invalidate their refutation of MOND. Gallardo’s team openly admits they ignored this effect, believing it negligible—but that’s still open for debate.

Regardless, general relativity and the theory of dark matter are coming out looking stronger than ever. In fact, the ACT data amounts to the most extensive test of Einstein’s relativistic gravity theory ever performed.

The Legendary Sunyaev-Zel’dovich Effect

The Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect, first theorized by the Russian cosmologists Rashid Sunyaev and Yakov Zel’dovich in the late 1960s and observed directly in 1983, is now almost as famous as the Big Bang itself among astronomers.

So, what does this effect actually do? Sunyaev and Zel’dovich realized that a gas of hot electrons, common in many astrophysical situations, would subject CMB photons to the inverse Compton effect. The result: photons collide with high-energy electrons in hot plasma, boosting some to higher energies. The upshot is a deficit of low-energy photons and a surplus at higher energies. The classic blackbody spectrum of the cosmic microwave background is thus visibly distorted—pushed toward higher frequencies on scientific charts, as shown above.

So, has the cosmic microwave background just destroyed the leading dark matter alternative? The cosmic jury is still deliberating, with a few surprises left—but it’s safe to say the evidence for both general relativity and dark matter has never looked brighter. Or, paradoxically, darker.
